# ![[Uncaptioned image]](2610.32101v1/figs/prism_8132015.png) PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation

Qixin Xu    Zihan Zhu Affiliation: Tsinghua University.    Xiaojiang Liu
Affiliation: Apple.    Bohan Lyu Email: [xqx23@mails.tsinghua.edu.cn,
lyubh22@gmail.com^(\*)Equal contribution](mailto:Equal%20contribution)
Affiliation: Corresponding author

###### Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) exhibit _mode collapse_, where their output
distribution concentrates on familiar semantic modes. When diversity
disappears, repeated sampling becomes semantic repetition rather than
discovery, making rare but stronger solutions unlikely to surface and
leaving self-evolution and continual learning difficult to sustain. Most
remedies intervene only at inference time, shaping samples without
making diversity a model capability. We propose PRISM, a training-time
framework that internalizes diversity within the model. PRISM combines
(i) _submodular curation_ that pairs each prompt with
diverse-yet-correct multi-teacher solutions, and (ii) _stochastic
embedding modulation_, which turns special-token perturbations into
implicit signals for sampling distinct outputs. A theoretical analysis
establishes the stability of this mechanism. On WritingPrompts and
BookMIA, PRISM moves the quality-diversity frontier outward, achieving
the best generation quality in all model-benchmark settings while
maintaining the strongest or near-strongest semantic diversity across
two open-weight model families. It also improves sampling efficiency on
math and code benchmarks. Beyond inference, PRISM yields a stronger
foundation for reinforcement learning, sustaining diverse rollouts and
mitigating the diversity collapse commonly observed during RL training.

## 1 Introduction

Post-trained large language models (LLMs) exhibit _mode collapse_, where
their output distribution concentrates on a small set of familiar
semantic modes ([Padmakumar and He, 2024](#bib.bib48); [West and Potts,
2025](#bib.bib49); [Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib45); [Lanchantin et
al., 2025](#bib.bib51)). This collapse weakens the model’s ability to
use sampling as exploration: repeated samples revisit the same
trajectories, making rare but stronger outputs harder to discover and
limiting the rollout diversity needed for self-improvement. The effect
appears in both open-ended generation, where outputs become
homogeneous ([Lu et al., 2025](#bib.bib50); [Zhang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib45); [Jiang et al., 2025](#bib.bib46)), and verifiable
reasoning, where near-identical solution paths reduce the gains from
scaled test-time compute ([Snell et al., 2024](#bib.bib3); [Muennighoff
et al., 2025](#bib.bib4); [Hooper et al., 2025](#bib.bib5); [Ju et al.,
2025](#bib.bib75); [Lyu et al., 2025a](#bib.bib84); [Wang et al.,
2024a](#bib.bib6); [Song et al., 2025](#bib.bib78)). Because diversity
loss can be shaped by post-training data and learned weights, not only
decoding choices ([Karouzos et al., 2026](#bib.bib52)), reducing mode
collapse is crucial for preserving a model’s capacity to explore,
discover, and self-evolve.

![Refer to caption](2610.32101v1/prism_teaser_0123.png)

Figure 1: Overview of PRISM. Left: Traditional SFT collapses onto a
single dominant trajectory. Middle: PRISM internalizes diversity through
submodular curation of diverse-yet-correct trajectories and stochastic
embedding modulation that perturbs the prompt embedding with Gaussian
noise. Right: At inference, different noise samples steer the model
toward distinct modes, producing diverse trajectories from the same
prompt.

Existing methods for improving LLM output diversity fall into several
families, but they rarely make diversity something the model can be
steered to produce on demand. _Inference-time methods_, including
token-level decoding strategies ([Vijayakumar et al., 2016](#bib.bib9);
[Ippolito et al., 2019](#bib.bib8); [Meister et al., 2023](#bib.bib11)),
prompt-based interventions ([Naik et al., 2023](#bib.bib7); [Zhang et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib45); [Wong et al., 2025](#bib.bib53); [Ruan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib54); [Santos et al., 2025](#bib.bib55)), search-based
methods ([Mouret and Clune, 2015](#bib.bib56); [Romera-Paredes et al.,
2024](#bib.bib62); [Novikov et al., 2025](#bib.bib63); [He et al.,
2026](#bib.bib65)), and latent or decoding-space alternatives ([Geiping
et al., 2025](#bib.bib39); [Zhang et al., 2025c](#bib.bib40); [Chen et
al., 2025](#bib.bib41)), try to force variation at generation time.
Because the model itself has not learned when and how to vary its
answers, these methods can stop at surface-level changes or spend extra
tokens for each prompt. _Training-time noise methods_, in contrast, do
modify the model itself, but typically inject noise into embeddings as a
generic regularizer ([Jain et al., 2023b](#bib.bib44); [Yadav and Singh,
2023](#bib.bib73); [Zhu et al., 2019](#bib.bib15)), improving
instruction-following or robustness without making diversity
controllable. Recent data-centric and multi-solution training methods
improve coverage, especially in reasoning and code, but they largely
decide which traces to train on or how to label modes ([Wang et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib74); [Ju et al., 2025](#bib.bib75); [Just et al.,
2025](#bib.bib76); [Jia et al., 2026](#bib.bib77)). The remaining gap is
a model-level mechanism that lets the same prompt produce different
valid outputs through an internal control signal.

To this end, we propose PRISM, a training-time framework that teaches
LLMs to use a small internal signal to choose among multiple valid
outputs for the same prompt. PRISM has two coupled components: one
defines _what_ diverse outputs the model should learn, and the other
gives the model a way to move among them. First, we build specialized
training datasets via submodular curation, in which each prompt is
paired with multiple diverse-yet-correct solutions drawn from a
multi-teacher candidate pool; this defines the _target space_ of valid
output trajectories the model should be able to produce. Second, we
inject Gaussian noise into a small set of special-token embeddings
during both training and inference; under the curated supervision
provided by the first component, different noise samples become _learned
navigation signals_ that steer the model toward distinct trajectories
within this target space, rather than acting as generic regularization.
We provide a theoretical analysis showing that this noise injection is
provably stable and can be interpreted as a regularizer on the Hessian
of the loss with respect to embeddings.

We center our evaluation on open-ended creative writing, where diversity
must be semantic rather than merely lexical. On WritingPrompts and
BookMIA across two open-weight model families, PRISM achieves the best
generation quality in all model-benchmark settings and the strongest or
near-strongest semantic diversity among competitive inference-time and
training-time baselines. These results shift the quality-diversity
frontier outward rather than trading one axis for the other. We further
evaluate PRISM on verifiable math and code reasoning, where it improves
sampling efficiency by discovering more correct solutions under
equivalent inference budgets.

For reinforcement learning (RL) post-training, diversity determines what
behaviors the policy can still explore: once rollouts collapse, reward
feedback comes from repeated variants of the same solution and policy
improvement stalls ([Cui et al., 2025b](#bib.bib30); [Cui et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib86); [Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib31); [Xu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib87)). By exposing multiple correct modes through a
controllable sampling interface, PRISM lets RL train on a wider range of
rollouts; in math and code reasoning, this preserves diversity during
training and avoids the sampling collapse observed with standard SFT
initialization.

In conclusion, our main contributions are:

- •
  We introduce PRISM, a training-time framework that pairs per-prompt
  submodular curation with stochastic special-token embeddings to make
  diversity controllable at inference.
- •
  We show that PRISM improves the quality-diversity frontier on creative
  writing tasks on two open-weight models.
- •
  We demonstrate stronger sampling-based exploration on eight math and
  code benchmarks, discovering more correct solutions than SFT and prior
  diversity-enhancing baselines under the same inference budgets.
- •
  We show that diversity supports policy improvement: PRISM checkpoints
  preserve exploratory rollouts during RL and help the policy continue
  discovering correct programs.

## 2 Methodology

Our methodology aims to enable LLMs to generate diverse yet correct
reasoning trajectories. We first construct diverse training datasets
using submodular optimization to sample varied reasoning paths
(Section [2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 Diverse Reasoning Trajectory Sampling via Submodular Optimization ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation")),
then train and do inference with the model with noisy special-token
embeddings
(Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Noisy Special-token Embeddings as Implicit Diversity Signals ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation")).
We provide analysis on our training target to understand its impact
(Section [2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 Training Target Analysis ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation")).

### 2.1 Diverse Reasoning Trajectory Sampling via Submodular Optimization

Following prior work on diversity as feature coverage in summarization
and data selection ([Filatova and Hatzivassiloglou, 2004](#bib.bib22);
[Takamura and Okumura, 2009](#bib.bib23); [Lin and Bilmes,
2011](#bib.bib24)), we define the diversity of a subset $`A\subseteq S`$
as the number of distinct reasoning features it covers:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       f(A)=\left|\bigcup_{s_{a}\in A}F(s_{a})\right|,
       ```                                              |     | (1) |

where $`F(s_{a})`$ denotes the set of discrete reasoning features of
trajectory $`s_{a}`$. Feature construction is per-domain: for creative
writing, we embed candidate completions with SBERT and cluster them,
using cluster IDs as the discrete feature set; for math, features are
n-grams over solution tokens; for code, n-grams together with AST
subtrees.
Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Feature Engineering from Reasoning Trajectories ‣ Appendix A Submodular Optimization for Diverse Trajectory Sampling ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation")
details each construction.

To maximize this diversity under a budget constraint, we adopt a
two-stage framework. First, for each input, we collect a candidate set
of $`m`$ trajectories, $`S=\{s_{1},\dots,s_{m}\}`$. Second, we employ a
submodular subset optimization strategy ([Krause and Golovin,
2014](#bib.bib18)) to extract a fixed-size subset $`A\subseteq S`$ of
$`n`$ trajectories that maximizes $`f(A)`$.

We use a greedy algorithm to maximize $`f(A)`$ subject to $`|A|=n`$.
Starting with an empty set $`A_{0}=\emptyset`$, at each step $`t`$
($`t=0,\dots,n-1`$), we select trajectory $`s_{t+1}`$ that offers the
largest marginal gain:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
s_{t+1}=\underset{s_{i}\in S\setminus A_{t}}{\arg\max}\big(f(A_{t}\cup\{s_{i}\})-f(A_{t})\big).
``` |  | (2) |

Let $`U_{t}=\bigcup_{s_{a}\in A_{t}}F(s_{a})`$ denote the features
already covered. The criterion simplifies to:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
s_{t+1}=\underset{s_{i}\in S\setminus A_{t}}{\arg\max}\;\big|F(s_{i})\setminus U_{t}\big|.
``` |  | (3) |

This algorithm guarantees a $`1-1/e`$ approximation to the optimal
feature coverage achievable with $`n`$ samples ([Nemhauser et al.,
1978](#bib.bib17)).
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Submodular Optimization for Diverse Trajectory Sampling ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation")
further explains it. We further validate the selected training data with
human annotations on 32 code and math queries. As shown in
Table [1](#S2.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 2.1 Diverse Reasoning Trajectory Sampling via Submodular Optimization ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation"),
submodular selection produces more queries with at least three distinct
solutions than random sampling; annotation details are in
Appendix [H](#A8 "Appendix H Human Check Results ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation").

| Datasets                    | $`\geq 3`$ | $`2`$    | $`1`$    |
|-----------------------------|------------|----------|----------|
| Code                        | $`34.4`$   | $`37.5`$ | $`28.1`$ |
| w/o submodular optimization | $`25.0`$   | $`37.5`$ | $`37.5`$ |
| Math                        | $`42.8`$   | $`39.3`$ | $`17.9`$ |
| w/o submodular optimization | $`28.1`$   | $`37.5`$ | $`34.4`$ |

### 2.2 Noisy Special-token Embeddings as Implicit Diversity Signals

While traditional SFT learns a direct mapping between inputs and
outputs, it does not account for the need to generate diverse yet
correct outputs for the same input. To foster diversity-controllable
sampling, we hope to control the models to produce different valid
reasoning paths.

To achieve this, we introduce Gaussian noise perturbations to the
embeddings of special input tokens during both training and inference.
Let $`x=(x_{1},\dots,x_{L})`$ be the token IDs of an input sequence. The
standard sequence of embedding vectors for $`x`$ is
$`\mathbf{E}_{x}=(\mathbf{e}_{x_{1}},\dots,\mathbf{e}_{x_{L}})`$. We
define a corresponding noise sequence
$`\mathbf{N}_{x}=(\mathbf{n}_{x_{1}},\dots,\mathbf{n}_{x_{L}})`$. For
each position $`j`$, the noise vector $`\mathbf{n}_{x_{j}}`$ is sampled
from $`\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\sigma^{2}\mathbf{I})`$ if $`x_{j}`$ is a
special token, and $`\mathbf{n}_{x_{j}}=\mathbf{0}`$ if $`x_{j}`$ is
not. This targeted noise injection perturbs the input representation at
specific special token positions, thereby stimulating diverse model
outputs while keeping the core semantic information of the input
sequence $`x`$ intact. The effective input embedding sequence to the
model, $`\mathbf{E}^{\prime}_{x}`$, is the element-wise sum of the two
parts:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbf{E}^{\prime}_{x}=\mathbf{E}_{x}+\mathbf{N}_{x}=(\mathbf{e}_{x_{1}}+\mathbf{n}_{x_{1}},\dots,\mathbf{e}_{x_{L}}+\mathbf{n}_{x_{L}}).
``` |  | (4) |

The training objective is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{J}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x,\,y\sim A(x),\,\mathbf{N}_{x}}\left[-\log p_{\theta}(y\mid\mathbf{E}^{\prime}_{x})\right]
``` |  | (5) |

where $`A(x)`$ is the curated answer set from
Section [2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 Diverse Reasoning Trajectory Sampling via Submodular Optimization ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation")
and $`\mathbf{N}_{x}`$ is freshly sampled per forward pass. Because the
same $`x`$ is paired with multiple $`y\in A(x)`$ under different
$`\mathbf{N}_{x}`$ over the course of training, noise-conditioned
solutions that commit to different valid answers under different draws
attain the same expected loss as any noise-invariant one, and training
settles on the former: the model learns to treat the noise as an
implicit selector among valid answers. At inference, varying
$`\mathbf{N}_{x}`$ then yields varying $`y`$.

### 2.3 Training Target Analysis

We conduct theoretical analyses to answer two questions: (1) Does
injecting noise into special-token embeddings destabilize the language
model? (2) How does our training formulation facilitate controllable
diversity at inference time?

##### Embeddings.

For the embeddings, the introduction of Gaussian noise acts as a form of
regularization. Formally, let the vocabulary size be $`V`$ and the
embedding dimension be $`D`$. The embedding matrix is denoted as
$`\mathbf{E}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times D}`$. $`\mathbf{E}^{\prime}`$ is the
embedding added with randomly sampled Gaussian Noise. Analyzing the
expected loss function
$`\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{n}}[L(\mathbf{E}^{\prime})]`$ reveals that it
introduces an regularization term:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{n}}[L(\mathbf{E}^{\prime})]=L(\mathbf{E})+\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}\text{tr}(\mathbf{H}_{i})+O(\sigma^{3}),
``` |  | (6) |

where $`\mathbf{H}_{i}`$ is the Hessian of the loss function with
respect to the embedding $`\mathbf{e}_{i}`$. This term, proportional to
the trace of the Hessian, is a style of regularization ([Bishop,
1995](#bib.bib16)) by penalizing high-curvature regions of the loss
landscape. This justifies the noise injection as a principled
regularizer, contributing a well-behaved smoothing term to the expected
loss. See
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Proof of the Regularization Effect of Noise Injection ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation")
for a detailed derivation.

##### Language Model.

We can decompose the per-instance log-probability term in
Equation [5](#S2.E5 "In 2.2 Noisy Special-token Embeddings as Implicit Diversity Signals ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation")
as (noting that $`y\in A(x)`$ by construction):

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle p_{\theta}(y\mid\mathbf{E}^{\prime}_{x})=`$ |  | (7) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle p_{\theta}\bigl(Y=y\mid Y\in A(x),\mathbf{E}^{\prime}_{x}\bigr)\cdot p_{\theta}\bigl(Y\in A(x)\mid\mathbf{E}^{\prime}_{x}\bigr).`$ |  |  |

Taking the negative logarithm, the per-instance loss decomposes into a
component ensuring general answer correctness and another that promotes
the noise-conditioned selection of specific diverse answers:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  |  | $`\displaystyle-\log p_{\theta}(y\mid\mathbf{E}^{\prime}_{x})=-\underbrace{\log\Bigl(\sum\nolimits_{y^{\prime}\in A(x)}p_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid\mathbf{E}^{\prime}_{x})\Bigr)}_{\text{Semantic Correctness}}`$ |  | (8) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle-\underbrace{\log p_{\theta}\bigl(Y=y\mid Y\in A(x),\mathbf{E}^{\prime}_{x}\bigr)}_{\text{Noise-Conditioned Specificity}}.`$ |  |  |

The semantic correctness term ensures that the model consistently
generates outputs from the set of correct solutions. The
noise-conditioned specificity term is minimized by solutions that use
the injected noise as a control signal to select a particular trajectory
from the correct set, and our ablations in Section 3.1 confirm training
converges to such a solution. At test time, by varying the noise
injected, we can flexibly generate diverse valid outputs for the same
input, thus achieving test-time scaling. A detailed explanation of this
part is provided in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Detailed Analysis of the Loss Objective Decomposition ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation").

## 3 Experiments

We evaluate PRISM on two complementary task families: open-ended
creative writing
(Section [3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Creative Writing ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation")),
where quality is assessed jointly with diversity, and verifiable
reasoning on math and code
(Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Math and Code Reasoning ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation")),
where sampling efficiency is measured by Pass@N. We then evaluate the
PRISM as a beneficial foundation for RL
(Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Reinforcement Learning ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation")).

### 3.1 Creative Writing

##### Setup.

We use two long-form benchmarks: WritingPrompts ([Fan et al.,
2018](#bib.bib42)), where each Reddit-style prompt asks the model to
write a full short story, and BookMIA ([Shi et al., 2023](#bib.bib43)),
where the model continues a passage from the opening sentences of a
book. Both yield outputs of 800–2000 tokens, leaving sufficient room for
the noise-induced diversity signal to accumulate across plot decisions.
For each benchmark we sample 100 test prompts and generate $`N=30`$
responses per prompt with target length 800 words. We evaluate two
open-weight instruction-tuned models from different families,
Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, and compare PRISM against
five baselines spanning inference-time and training-time: Vanilla
sampling, standard SFT, NEFTune ([Jain et al., 2023b](#bib.bib44)),
VS-Standard ([Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib45)), and FIRE ([Chen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib41)). Details and hyperparameters are in appendix
[D](#A4 "Appendix D Evaluation Details ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation").

Figure 2: Pass@N performance of PRISM, SFT, and Base models under
different temperatures. PRISM’s gain is consistent across temperatures.

##### Training Data.

Training prompts are drawn from the WritingPrompts training split ([Fan
et al., 2018](#bib.bib42)) and the BookMIA training split ([Shi et al.,
2023](#bib.bib43)), yielding 10000 prompts in total; the benchmark test
prompts used for evaluation are held out throughout. For each training
prompt, we follow the submodular selection pipeline detailed in
(Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Math and Code Reasoning ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation")),
details are listed in appendix
[7](#A6.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Framework. ‣ Appendix F Fintune Backbone Details ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation").

##### Evaluation.

Following [Zhang et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib45), we measure diversity as
$`1-\bar{s}`$ (%), where $`\bar{s}`$ is the mean pairwise cosine
similarity of within-prompt response embeddings under OpenAI
text-embedding-3-small (negative similarities clipped to $`0`$). Quality
is the Creative Writing v3 rubric ([Paech, 2025](#bib.bib47)) score
(0–100) judged by Claude-3.7-Sonnet and GPT-4o. Higher is better on both
axes.

##### Results.

Table [2](#S2.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Language Model. ‣ 2.3 Training Target Analysis ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation")
reports diversity and quality across both benchmarks and both model
families. PRISM achieves the highest quality in all four (model,
benchmark) cells and strictly Pareto-dominates Vanilla, SFT, NEFTune,
and FIRE in every cell. GEM is the strongest diversity baseline on Qwen,
exceeding PRISM by at most 1.3 points of diversity at a cost of 1.6 to
6.4 points of quality; on Llama, PRISM is higher than GEM on both axes
in both benchmarks. VS-Standard similarly exceeds PRISM by at most 1.8
diversity points while giving up 5 to 8 points of quality. Across all
four cells, PRISM thus shifts the quality-diversity Pareto frontier
outward rather than trading along it.

##### Ablations.

We evaluate four variants: (i) w/o Noise (curated data only, no noise),
(ii) w/o Div (noise on both sides but randomly sampled training data),
(iii) w/o InN (full training, no noise at inference), and (iv) SFT w/
InN (the SFT checkpoint with the same noise injected only at inference),
which completes the 2×2 factorial over training-time and inference-time
noise. The four comparisons attribute the gains component by component.
Curation defines the modes: replacing curated data with random sampling
(w/o Div) drops diversity by 3.6 to 4.6 points with noise fully in
place. Curated data alone does not realize the gains: training on the
same data without noise (w/o Noise) loses 6 to 9 points of quality
relative to PRISM. Training-time noise is what makes the perturbation
usable: injected into a checkpoint never trained under it (SFT w/ InN),
the same noise raises diversity but costs 3 to 6 points of quality,
while under the noise-trained checkpoint it raises both. Finally, the
mechanism requires inference-time activation: with identical training,
w/o InN forfeits both the remaining diversity and a substantial quality
margin (45.4 to 51.0 on Qwen WritingPrompts), showing that the noise
functions as an inference-time conditioning signal rather than a
training regularizer whose effect would already be in the weights.

### 3.2 Math and Code Reasoning

##### Setup.

We evaluate on eight reasoning benchmarks: four code (HumanEval, MBPP,
HumanEval+, MBPP+ ([Chen et al., 2021](#bib.bib32); [Austin et al.,
2021](#bib.bib34); [Liu et al., 2023](#bib.bib33))) and four math
(MATH-500 ([Hendrycks et al., 2021](#bib.bib20); [Lightman et al.,
2024](#bib.bib35)), AMC23, AIME 24/25 ([Mathematical Association of
America, 2024](#bib.bib27); [Mathematical Association of America,
2025](#bib.bib28))). The experiments are built on Llama-3.1-8B-Base with
a warm-up SFT on Ultra-Chat ([Ding et al., 2023](#bib.bib36)) and
reasoning data distilled from Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.

##### Training Data.

For math, we sample 10000 problems from A-m-team verified data ([Tian et
al., 2025](#bib.bib37)) with mid-range cross-model accuracy
($`33\%`$–$`67\%`$) and use n-gram submodular optimization to select 4
diverse answers per problem. For code, we draw from four sources:
A-m-team distilled solutions, LeetCode problems, OpenCoder SFT-Stage-2
educational-instruct ([Huang et al., 2024](#bib.bib21)) solutions, and a
broader OpenCoder mix for general coding ability. Code submodular
selection uses both n-gram and AST features. Baseline datasets randomly
sample 4 solutions per problem to control for token count. Full data
preparation details are in appendix
[7](#A6.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Framework. ‣ Appendix F Fintune Backbone Details ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation").

##### Evaluation.

We report Pass@N using the standard unbiased estimator ([Chen et al.,
2021](#bib.bib32)). Given $`M`$ generated samples with $`c`$ correct
ones, Pass@$`k`$ is estimated as $`1-\binom{M-c}{k}/\binom{M}{k}`$ and
averaged across all problems in each dataset.

##### Results.

Table [3](#S2.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Language Model. ‣ 2.3 Training Target Analysis ‣ 2 Methodology ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation")
shows PRISM attains the highest Pass@N on seven of the eight benchmarks,
with AIME 2025 tied with SFT and NEFTune higher on MBPP+. Against Base,
PRISM lifts AIME 2024 from 6.67 to 23.33 on a benchmark where mode
collapse is most punitive. Against SFT, which already absorbs the
benefit of supervised distillation, PRISM still delivers consistent
further gains, including +13.33 on AIME 2024 and +10.0 on AMC 23.
NEFTune, which injects noise only during training as a regularizer, also
improves clearly over SFT, consistent with the robustness effect of
training-time noise; the remaining gap to PRISM, largest on AIME 2024
where trajectory diversity matters most, is what inference-time
conditioning adds.
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Setup. ‣ 3.1 Creative Writing ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation")
further shows these gains hold across temperatures, confirming that
PRISM’s mechanism is complementary to, rather than redundant with,
temperature scaling.

##### Ablations.

We evaluate the w/o Noise, w/o Div, and w/o InN variants on the
reasoning benchmarks. Each component alone is insufficient: w/o Noise
improves over SFT on math but is flat on code, and w/o Div lifts math
further yet underperforms SFT on several code benchmarks. More
importantly, inference-time noise is what activates the learned
diversity signal: w/o InN consistently underperforms full PRISM despite
sharing identical training (AIME 2024 pass@64: 16.67 vs. 23.33),
confirming that the noise vector functions as a learned navigation
signal exercised at test time rather than a training-time regularizer.

### 3.3 Reinforcement Learning

##### Setup.

RL training is particularly vulnerable to rollout-diversity collapse,
where decreasing policy entropy stalls improvement ([Cui et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib30); [Lin et al., 2025](#bib.bib38)). We test whether
PRISM’s training-time diversity carries into RL by initializing
veRL ([Sheng et al., 2025](#bib.bib29)) from two checkpoints, SFT, and
full PRISM, and training on SimpleRL-Zoo ([Zeng et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib25)) for math and Acecoder-V2 ([Zeng et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib26)) for code. The full PRISM run additionally injects
noise during RL rollouts. Details of RL training are in
Appendix [G](#A7 "Appendix G RL Training Details ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation").

##### Results.

Table [4](#S3.T4 "Table 4 ‣ Ablations. ‣ 3.2 Math and Code Reasoning ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation")
compares pre- and post-RL pass@64 across math and code; AIME averages
AIME 2024 and AIME 2025. Two findings stand out. First, PRISM provides a
uniformly stronger RL initialization: both pre-RL and post-RL pass@64
are higher than SFT in every cell, indicating that the diversity
inherited from PRISM persists as a more productive search space
throughout RL. Second, math and code respond asymmetrically. On math,
both SFT and PRISM improve after RL. On code, SFT loses pass@64 across
all four settings (HumanEval/+ at both temperatures), whereas PRISM
improves on three of four code cells and drops only marginally on
HumanEval+ at $`T{=}0.3`$. PRISM thus appears to prevent the high-pass
collapse commonly observed during RL fine-tuning. We attribute the
math–code asymmetry to the distinct distributional shifts each task
imposes between SFT and RL training data.

## 4 Analyses

### 4.1 Other Diversity Enhancing Baselines

We also compare our methods with other methods that focus on reasoning
diversity on code tasks.

##### Baselines.

\(1\) Diverse Beam Search (DBS) ([Vijayakumar et al., 2016](#bib.bib9)):
A beam search-based method that optimizes a diversity-augmented
objective. We applied DBS to both Llama-3.1-8B-Base with warm-up and
Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. (2) GEM ([Li et al., 2024](#bib.bib13)): GEM is
an SFT algorithm that prevents over-memorization and promotes diversity
in the model’s outputs. We applied GEM to Llama-3.1-8B-Base with
randomly-sampled training data and default training parameters.

##### Results.

As shown in
Table [5](#S4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Results. ‣ 4.1 Other Diversity Enhancing Baselines ‣ 4 Analyses ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation"),
our analysis reveals several key findings. (1) DBS consistently degrades
performance on both base and instruct models. It results in lower scores
across all Pass@1 and Pass@N metrics compared to its respective original
model. (2) PRISM demonstrates superior performance especially at higher
sampling budgets. While GEM performs well on HumanEval, our method
achieves the highest Pass@64 scores on the other three benchmarks,
outperforming both GEM and the extensively trained Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct
model.

| Method | HumanEval | HumanEval+ | MBPP | MBPP+ |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| Base | $`81.14`$ | $`72.89`$ | $`75.42`$ | $`69.99`$ |
| w/ DBS | $`62.58`$ | $`56.10`$ | $`66.40`$ | $`61.64`$ |
| Instruct | $`\underline{88.49}`$ | $`\underline{83.27}`$ | $`\underline{86.05}`$ | $`\underline{76.42}`$ |
| w/ DBS | $`79.75`$ | $`73.17`$ | $`85.45`$ | $`74.87`$ |
| GEM | $`\mathbf{89.57}`$ | $`82.32`$ | $`84.13`$ | $`75.66`$ |
| PRISM | $`87.81`$ | $`\mathbf{83.82}`$ | $`\mathbf{86.11}`$ | $`\mathbf{77.26}`$ |

Table 5: Pass@64 performance on code benchmarks. PRISM demonstrates
superior sampling efficiency compared with both GEM and DBS.

### 4.2 Sourcing the Effectiveness of PRISM

To elucidate how PRISM improves Pass@N performance in reasoning task, we
conduct analyses on code tasks. We annotate the algorithms utilized in
the solutions generated by PRISM and SFT models: we firstly categorize
all possible solution algorithms into 39 classes and employ the Qwen3-8B
model to automatically label each generated solution. The details for
labeling are in
Appendix [I](#A9 "Appendix I LLM-As-Judge Pipeline ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation").

##### PRISM Enhances Algorithmic Diversity.

For each query, we compute the change in both unique algorithm count and
Pass@N score between PRISM and SFT. As shown in
Figure [3](#S4.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ PRISM Enhances Algorithmic Diversity. ‣ 4.2 Sourcing the Effectiveness of PRISM ‣ 4 Analyses ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation"),
PRISM consistently shifts the distribution towards a higher count of
unique algorithms per query, which indicates a greater algorithm-level
diversity in its outputs compared to SFT.

Figure 3: Distribution of unique algorithm counts per query for SFT and
PRISM. PRISM’s shifts toward higher counts, indicating greater
algorithmic diversity.

##### Algorithmic Diversity Drives Test-Time Scaling.

We then statistically examine the link between this enhanced diversity
and performance gains. For each query, we compute the delta in both the
unique algorithm count and the Pass@N score between the PRISM and SFT
models. As illustrated in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Algorithmic Diversity Drives Test-Time Scaling. ‣ 4.2 Sourcing the Effectiveness of PRISM ‣ 4 Analyses ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation"),
queries where PRISM produces more distinct algorithms ($`+`$) gain
substantially on Pass@N, the gap widens from Pass@64 to Pass@128.
Algorithmic diversity is thus a primary driver of PRISM’s test-time
scaling, with the benefit amplified at larger sample budgets.

Figure 4: Change in Pass@N versus change in unique algorithm count per
query (both PRISM minus SFT), grouped into decrease (-), unchanged (0),
and increase (+). Error bars show standard error of the mean.

## 5 Related Work

##### Mode Collapse in LLMs.

Post-training, including SFT and RL, can improve helpfulness or
correctness while making generations more repetitive and less
varied ([Padmakumar and He, 2024](#bib.bib48); [West and Potts,
2025](#bib.bib49); [Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib45); [Lanchantin et
al., 2025](#bib.bib51)). Recent analyses trace much of the loss to
post-training data and learned weights ([Karouzos et al.,
2026](#bib.bib52)). The effect appears in open-ended prompts as
repetition and cross-model homogeneity ([Lu et al., 2025](#bib.bib50);
[Jiang et al., 2025](#bib.bib46)), and in verifiable reasoning as
repeated solution patterns that limit gains from scaled sampling ([Ju et
al., 2025](#bib.bib75); [Wang et al., 2024a](#bib.bib6); [Song et al.,
2025](#bib.bib78)).

##### Inference-Time and Search-Based Diversity.

Many methods try to recover diversity only at inference time, including
decoding, prompt-based, and guidance-based methods ([Vijayakumar et al.,
2016](#bib.bib9); [Holtzman et al., 2019](#bib.bib10); [Meister et al.,
2023](#bib.bib11); [Ippolito et al., 2019](#bib.bib8); [Zhang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib45); [Wong et al., 2025](#bib.bib53); [Ruan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib54); [Santos et al., 2025](#bib.bib55)). More structured
search methods maintain archives or populations of high-scoring but
behaviorally distinct candidates ([Mouret and Clune, 2015](#bib.bib56);
[Lehman et al., 2022](#bib.bib57); [Meyerson et al., 2023](#bib.bib58);
[Lim et al., 2024](#bib.bib59); [Bradley et al., 2023](#bib.bib60);
[Samvelyan et al., 2024](#bib.bib61)). In reasoning, code, and math,
this becomes evaluator-guided program search, mathematical discovery,
reward-guided diverse reasoning, behavioral clustering, or parallel
thought generation ([Romera-Paredes et al., 2024](#bib.bib62); [Novikov
et al., 2025](#bib.bib63); [Younsi et al., 2025](#bib.bib64); [He et
al., 2026](#bib.bib65); [Wen et al., 2025](#bib.bib66); [Geiping et al.,
2025](#bib.bib39); [Zhang et al., 2025c](#bib.bib40); [Chen et al.,
2025](#bib.bib41); [Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib89); [Zhang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib88)). These methods improve exploration, but the diversity
comes from prompts, decoders, archives, or external evaluators.

##### Training-Time Approaches for Diversity.

Existing training-time methods usually treat data construction and model
control separately. Embedding-noise methods use perturbations as
regularization, encouraging robustness to noise rather than using noise
to steer outputs ([Jain et al., 2023b](#bib.bib44); [Yadav and Singh,
2023](#bib.bib73); [Zhu et al., 2019](#bib.bib15); [Bishop,
1995](#bib.bib16)). Data-centric methods improve coverage through
attributes, submodular mixtures, utility pruning, quality-diversity
generation, or gradient-space selection ([Chung et al.,
2023](#bib.bib67); [Yu et al., 2023](#bib.bib68); [Renduchintala et al.,
2024](#bib.bib69); [Agarwal et al., 2024](#bib.bib70); [Havrilla et al.,
2025](#bib.bib71); [Jung et al., 2025](#bib.bib72); [Filatova and
Hatzivassiloglou, 2004](#bib.bib22); [Takamura and Okumura,
2009](#bib.bib23); [Lin and Bilmes, 2011](#bib.bib24); [Yuan et al.,
2023](#bib.bib12)). Recent reasoning and code work makes the point
sharper: one-problem-one-solution supervision misses many valid paths,
but simply adding more traces is not enough if training collapses them
into one dominant mode ([Wang et al., 2024b](#bib.bib74); [Ju et al.,
2025](#bib.bib75); [Just et al., 2025](#bib.bib76); [Jia et al.,
2026](#bib.bib77)).

##### Diversity in RL Post-Training.

RL post-training makes the same tension sharper. Outcome-only and
reverse-KL-style objectives can raise Pass@1 while narrowing rollouts,
hurting Pass@N and test-time scaling ([Song et al., 2025](#bib.bib78);
[Li et al., 2025a](#bib.bib79)). Recent RL methods therefore reward rare
outcomes, use mass-covering divergences, add token- or semantic-level
diversity rewards, or introduce count-based exploration ([Song et al.,
2025](#bib.bib78); [Li et al., 2025a](#bib.bib79); [Yao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib80); [Li et al., 2025b](#bib.bib81); [Zhang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib82)).

## 6 Conclusion

We presented PRISM, a framework that internalizes output diversity as a
controllable model capability via submodular data curation and
stochastic embedding modulation. On creative writing, PRISM shifts the
quality–diversity Pareto frontier outward, achieving the best generation
quality and the strongest semantic diversity. The same mechanism
transfers to verifiable reasoning, where PRISM consistently improves
Pass@N over SFT and prior diversity baselines, and to RL training, where
it provides a uniformly stronger foundation and prevents the high-pass
collapse commonly observed during standard RL post-training. These
results indicate that diversity, treated as a learnable training-time
signal rather than an inference-time intervention, can serve as a
unified mechanism.

Controllable diversity sets the foundation for continual
self-improvement ([Lyu et al., 2025b](#bib.bib83); [Lyu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib85)): by preserving exploratory rollouts, it keeps
sampling from degenerating into repetition and helps models discover
stronger candidates over time.

## Limitations

PRISM depends on a multi-solution candidate pool. For math and code we
draw on existing corpora, but for creative writing we constructed the
pool by repeated sampling from eight teacher models, a cost that recurs
in any domain without off-the-shelf multi-solution data. The noise scale
is task-dependent (sigma = 0.005 for writing, 0.01 for reasoning;
Appendix E), requiring a selection pass per task family. Our analysis
establishes stability but not diversity at the objective level: the
expected objective admits a noise-invariant optimum, and the routing
behavior we observe is a property of finite-step optimization,
characterized empirically rather than derived; making the noise
informative by construction is an open direction. Finally, evaluation
relies on LLM judges and a single embedding model, and our experiments
cover only 7B to 8B models.

  language models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2403.13372. Cited by: [Appendix

## Appendix A Submodular Optimization for Diverse Trajectory Sampling

### A.1 Feature Engineering from Reasoning Trajectories

The efficacy of our diversity framework hinges on a representation of
each candidate’s reasoning trajectory $`s_{k}\in S`$ through a set of
discrete “reasoning features,” denoted $`F(s_{k})`$. The nature of these
features is domain-specific. For natural language, such as textual
explanations or chains of thought, $`F(s_{k})`$ comprises the set of
unique n-grams constituting $`s_{k}`$. These n-grams serve as proxies
for local lexical, syntactic, and semantic patterns, allowing the
diversity metric to quantify the variety of expressed concepts and
phrasings. In the code generation, where trajectories might represent
sequences of operations or derived code structures, features
$`F(s_{k})`$ are extracted from Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs). Such
features capture the structural and logical idioms of the code, enabling
the selection of a functionally diverse set of trajectories. In all
cases, $`F(s_{k})`$ is a finite set of discrete elements for any given
$`s_{k}`$.

### A.2 The Submodular Optimization Problem

The core of our approach is the maximization of a set function
$`f:2^{S}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}`$, which quantifies the
diversity of a selected subset $`A\subseteq S`$. This objective is
defined as the total number of unique features covered by the
trajectories in $`A`$:

|     |                                                 |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       f(A)=\left|\bigcup_{s_{a}\in A}F(s_{a})\right|.
       ```                                              |     |

We now formally establish two key properties of this function:
monotonicity and submodularity.

##### Proposition 1.

The function $`f`$ is monotone non-decreasing.

###### Proof.

Consider any two sets $`A,B`$ such that $`A\subseteq B\subseteq S`$. By
the properties of the union operator, it follows directly that
$`\bigcup_{s_{a}\in A}F(s_{a})\subseteq\bigcup_{s_{b}\in B}F(s_{b})`$.
Taking the cardinality of both sides of this set inclusion, we obtain
$`\left|\bigcup_{s_{a}\in A}F(s_{a})\right|\leq\left|\bigcup_{s_{b}\in B}F(s_{b})\right|`$,
which by definition is $`f(A)\leq f(B)`$. ∎

##### Proposition 2.

The function $`f`$ is submodular.

###### Proof.

A set function $`f`$ is submodular if for any
$`X\subseteq Y\subseteq S`$ and any element $`s\in S\setminus Y`$, it
satisfies the condition of diminishing returns:
$`f(X\cup\{s\})-f(X)\geq f(Y\cup\{s\})-f(Y)`$. Let us examine the
marginal gain of adding an element $`s`$ to an arbitrary set
$`A\subseteq S`$. Define the covered feature set

|     |                                     |     |
|-----|-------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       U_{A}=\bigcup_{s_{a}\in A}F(s_{a}).
       ```                                  |     |

Then the gain is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle f(A\cup\{s\})-f(A)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\left|F(s)\cup U_{A}\right|-\left|U_{A}\right|`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\left|F(s)\setminus U_{A}\right|.`$ |  |

This is precisely the number of new features in $`s`$ that are not
already covered by the set $`A`$

Now, let $`U_{X}=\bigcup_{s_{x}\in X}F(s_{x})`$ and
$`U_{Y}=\bigcup_{s_{y}\in Y}F(s_{y})`$ be the feature sets covered by
$`X`$ and $`Y`$, respectively. The submodularity condition is equivalent
to proving that $`|F(s)\setminus U_{X}|\geq|F(s)\setminus U_{Y}|`$.

Since $`X\subseteq Y`$, we have $`U_{X}\subseteq U_{Y}`$. This implies
that any feature not covered by $`U_{Y}`$ is also not covered by
$`U_{X}`$. Formally, this gives the set inclusion
$`F(s)\setminus U_{Y}\subseteq F(s)\setminus U_{X}`$. Consequently,
their cardinalities must satisfy
$`|F(s)\setminus U_{Y}|\leq|F(s)\setminus U_{X}|`$. This concludes the
proof. ∎

1: Input: Candidate set of trajectories $`S=\{s_{1},\dots,s_{m}\}`$;
desired subset size $`n`$.

2: Input: Feature sets $`F(s_{k})`$ for each $`s_{k}\in S`$.

3: Output: A diverse subset $`A_{n}\subseteq S`$ of size $`n`$.

4: $`A\leftarrow\emptyset`$ $`\triangleright`$ Initialize selected set

5: $`U\leftarrow\emptyset`$ $`\triangleright`$ Initialize set of covered
features

6: for $`t\leftarrow 1\text{ to }n`$ do

7:   $`s^{*}\leftarrow\text{null}`$

8:   $`\text{max\_marginal\_gain}\leftarrow-1`$

9:   for each $`s_{i}\in S\setminus A`$ do

10:    $`\text{current\_gain}\leftarrow|F(s_{i})\setminus U|`$

11:    if $`\text{current\_gain}>\text{max\_marginal\_gain}`$ then

12:      $`\text{max\_marginal\_gain}\leftarrow\text{current\_gain}`$

13:      $`s^{*}\leftarrow s_{i}`$

14:    end if

15:   end for

16:   if $`s^{*}=\text{null}`$ and $`|A|<n`$ then

17:    $`\triangleright`$ No trajectory adds new features, or
$`S\setminus A`$ is empty. Pick any remaining from $`S\setminus A`$ if
needed to reach size $`n`$.

18:    $`s^{*}\leftarrow\text{any element from }S\setminus A`$

19:    if $`s^{*}=\text{null}`$ then

20:      break $`\triangleright`$ Cannot select more distinct items

21:    end if

22:   end if

23:   $`A\leftarrow A\cup\{s^{*}\}`$

24:   $`U\leftarrow U\cup F(s^{*})`$

25: end for

26: return $`A`$

Algorithm 1 Greedy Algorithm for Submodular Feature Coverage

### A.3 The Greedy Selection Algorithm

To select a subset $`A_{n}`$ of size $`n`$ that maximizes the defined
submodular function $`f(A)`$, we employ a standard greedy algorithm.
This iterative procedure builds the solution by repeatedly adding the
trajectory that offers the greatest marginal increase in $`f(A)`$
relative to the set of trajectories selected thus far.
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ Proposition 2. ‣ A.2 The Submodular Optimization Problem ‣ Appendix A Submodular Optimization for Diverse Trajectory Sampling ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation")
provides a formal pseudocode description of this process.

The algorithm iteratively identifies the trajectory $`s^{*}`$ that
contributes the largest number of features not yet present in the union
$`U`$ of features covered by trajectories already in $`A`$. The first
trajectory selected, $`s_{1}`$, is the one possessing the maximum number
of unique features, $`|F(s_{1})|`$. Each subsequent trajectory is chosen
based on its maximal contribution of new features to the evolving set
$`U`$.

### A.4 Theoretical Performance Guarantee and Its Significance

The utilization of a greedy strategy for maximizing a non-negative,
monotone, and submodular set function $`f(A)`$ subject to a uniform
cardinality constraint $`|A|\leq n`$ is well-justified by strong
theoretical results in combinatorial optimization. [Nemhauser et al.
(1978)](#bib.bib17) provides a constant-factor approximation guarantee
for this greedy algorithm. Specifically, the solution $`A_{n}`$ obtained
by the greedy algorithm satisfies $`f(A_{n})\geq(1-1/e)f(A_{OPT})`$,
where $`A_{OPT}`$ represents the true optimal subset of size $`n`$ that
maximizes $`f(A)`$.

## Appendix B Proof of the Regularization Effect of Noise Injection

Let $`\mathbf{E}`$ be the matrix of embedding parameters. We analyze the
effect of adding independent Gaussian noise
$`\mathbf{n}_{i}\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0},\sigma^{2}\mathbf{I})`$ to a
subset of embedding vectors $`\{\mathbf{e}_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{S}}`$,
where each $`\mathbf{e}_{i}`$ is a row in $`\mathbf{E}`$. The perturbed
embedding matrix is denoted by $`\mathbf{E}^{\prime}`$, where each
corresponding row is
$`\mathbf{e}^{\prime}_{i}=\mathbf{e}_{i}+\mathbf{n}_{i}`$. Our objective
is to compute the expected loss,
$`\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{N}}[L(\mathbf{E}^{\prime})]`$, where
$`\mathbf{N}=\{\mathbf{n}_{i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{S}}`$.

We perform a second-order Taylor expansion of the loss function
$`L(\mathbf{E}^{\prime})`$ around the noiseless matrix $`\mathbf{E}`$.
Let $`\mathbf{g}_{i}=\nabla_{\mathbf{e}_{i}}L(\mathbf{E})`$ and
$`\mathbf{H}_{ij}=\nabla_{\mathbf{e}_{i}}\nabla_{\mathbf{e}_{j}}L(\mathbf{E})`$
denote the gradient and Hessian blocks, respectively, evaluated at
$`\mathbf{E}`$. For notational convenience, we let
$`\mathbf{H}_{i}\equiv\mathbf{H}_{ii}`$. The expansion is given by:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
L(\mathbf{E}^{\prime})=L(\mathbf{E})+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}\mathbf{g}_{i}^{T}\mathbf{n}_{i}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j\in\mathcal{S}}\mathbf{n}_{i}^{T}\mathbf{H}_{ij}\mathbf{n}_{j}+O(\|\mathbf{N}\|^{3}).
``` |  | (9) |

We now take the expectation of each term with respect to the noise
distribution.

Since $`L(\mathbf{E})`$ is deterministic with respect to the noise,
$`\mathbb{E}[L(\mathbf{E})]=L(\mathbf{E})`$.

The linear term vanishes in expectation, as the noise has zero mean:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}\mathbf{g}_{i}^{T}\mathbf{n}_{i}\right]=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}\mathbf{g}_{i}^{T}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{n}_{i}]=\mathbf{0}.
``` |  | (10) |

For the quadratic term, we consider the diagonal ($`i=j`$) and
off-diagonal ($`i\neq j`$) components separately. For the off-diagonal
terms, the noise vectors $`\mathbf{n}_{i}`$ and $`\mathbf{n}_{j}`$ are
independent, hence:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{n}_{i}^{T}\mathbf{H}_{ij}\mathbf{n}_{j}\right]=\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{n}_{i}^{T}]\mathbf{H}_{ij}\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{n}_{j}]=\mathbf{0}^{T}\mathbf{H}_{ij}\mathbf{0}=0.
``` |  | (11) |

For the diagonal terms, we employ the cyclic property of the trace.
Recall that the covariance matrix of the noise is
$`\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{n}_{i}\mathbf{n}_{i}^{T}]=\sigma^{2}\mathbf{I}`$.

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\mathbf{n}_{i}^{T}\mathbf{H}_{i}\mathbf{n}_{i}\right]`$ | $`\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\text{tr}(\mathbf{H}_{i}\mathbf{n}_{i}\mathbf{n}_{i}^{T})\right]`$ |  | (12) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\text{tr}\left(\mathbf{H}_{i}\,\mathbb{E}[\mathbf{n}_{i}\mathbf{n}_{i}^{T}]\right)`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\text{tr}(\mathbf{H}_{i}(\sigma^{2}\mathbf{I}))`$ |  |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=\sigma^{2}\,\text{tr}(\mathbf{H}_{i}).`$ |  |  |

Finally, the expectation of the higher-order terms,
$`\mathbb{E}[O(\|\mathbf{N}\|^{3})]`$, is of order $`O(\sigma^{3})`$,
assuming sufficient smoothness of $`L`$.

Combining these results, we arrive at the expected loss:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{N}}[L(\mathbf{E}^{\prime})]=L(\mathbf{E})+\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{S}}\text{tr}(\mathbf{H}_{i})+O(\sigma^{3}).
``` |  | (13) |

## Appendix C Detailed Analysis of the Loss Objective Decomposition

The training objective is the minimization of the Negative
Log-Likelihood (NLL) loss over a joint distribution of inputs $`x`$,
targets $`y`$ drawn from the curated answer set $`A(x)`$, and noise
sequences $`\mathbf{N}_{x}`$ freshly sampled per forward pass. The model
is conditioned on a noisy input representation
$`\mathbf{E}^{\prime}_{x}=\mathbf{E}_{x}+\mathbf{N}_{x}`$, where
$`\mathbf{E}_{x}`$ is the noiseless embedding of $`x`$. The loss is:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{J}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x,\,y\sim A(x),\,\mathbf{N}_{x}}\left[-\log p_{\theta}(y\mid\mathbf{E}^{\prime}_{x})\right].
``` |  | (14) |

To understand the behavior induced by this objective, we decompose the
per-instance log-probability. Since $`y\in A(x)`$ by construction, we
apply the chain rule:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle p_{\theta}\bigl(Y=y\mid\mathbf{E}^{\prime}_{x}\bigr)`$ | $`\displaystyle=p_{\theta}\bigl(Y=y\mid Y\in A(x),\mathbf{E}^{\prime}_{x}\bigr)`$ |  | (15) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle\cdot p_{\theta}\bigl(Y\in A(x)\mid\mathbf{E}^{\prime}_{x}\bigr).`$ |  |  |

Taking the negative logarithm, the per-instance loss
$`L_{\text{inst.}}=-\log p_{\theta}(y\mid\mathbf{E}^{\prime}_{x})`$
separates into two additive components:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle L_{\text{inst.}}(x,y,\mathbf{N}_{x};\theta)`$ | $`\displaystyle=\underbrace{-\log p_{\theta}\bigl(Y\in A(x)\mid\mathbf{E}^{\prime}_{x}\bigr)}_{L_{C}(x,\mathbf{N}_{x};\,\theta)}`$ |  | (16) |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle+\underbrace{-\log p_{\theta}\bigl(Y=y\mid Y\in A(x),\mathbf{E}^{\prime}_{x}\bigr)}_{L_{D}(x,y,\mathbf{N}_{x};\,\theta)}.`$ |  |  |

Minimizing the total loss $`\mathcal{J}(\theta)`$ is thus equivalent to
jointly minimizing the expectation of these two terms.

##### The Semantic Correctness Component ($`L_{C}`$).

The first term depends on the total probability mass the model assigns
to the set of all correct answers:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
L_{C}(x,\mathbf{N}_{x};\theta)=-\log\!\left(\sum_{y^{\prime}\in A(x)}p_{\theta}(y^{\prime}\mid\mathbf{E}^{\prime}_{x})\right).
``` |  | (17) |

To minimize $`\mathbb{E}[L_{C}]`$, the model is incentivized to maximize
the collective probability of $`A(x)`$. This directly encourages the
model to learn the underlying semantic constraints of the task, ensuring
its generations are valid solutions.

##### The Noise-Conditioned Specificity Component ($`L_{D}`$).

The second term is the conditional log-likelihood of selecting the
specific target $`y`$ from within the set of correct answers:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
L_{D}(x,y,\mathbf{N}_{x};\theta)=-\log p_{\theta}\bigl(Y=y\mid Y\in A(x),\mathbf{E}^{\prime}_{x}\bigr).
``` |  | (18) |

Over the course of training, the same $`x`$ is paired with different
$`y\in A(x)`$ under independently sampled noise sequences
$`\mathbf{N}_{x}`$. Since $`\mathbf{N}_{x}`$ is independent of $`y`$, a
noise-invariant conditional matching the marginal over $`A(x)`$ attains
the optimal expected loss; however, noise-conditioned solutions that
commit to a single member of $`A(x)`$ per draw and average back to the
marginal attain near-identical expected loss, and are favored by
finite-step optimization: fitting the marginal requires per-token
predictions to hedge across all valid continuations where the curated
targets diverge, whereas committing per draw reduces the same loss more
readily. Training thus turns the injected noise into a control signal
for selecting among valid outputs. At inference, varying
$`\mathbf{N}_{x}`$ then yields varying $`y`$.

## Appendix D Evaluation Details

### D.1 Benchmarks

##### Creative Writing.

We evaluate on two long-form generation benchmarks. WritingPrompts ([Fan
et al., 2018](#bib.bib42)) is a story-generation dataset collected from
the Reddit r/WritingPrompts subreddit, where each prompt is a
one-sentence creative scenario and the model is asked to produce a full
short story. BookMIA ([Shi et al., 2023](#bib.bib43)) provides opening
passages from published books, and we task the model with continuing the
passage. For each benchmark, we sample 100 held-out test prompts
(disjoint from training prompts) and generate $`N=30`$ responses per
prompt with a target length of 800 words. Follow ([Paech,
2025](#bib.bib47)), we adopt Claude-3.7-Sonnet and GPT-4o as judge model
to evaluate the quality of model-generated answers.

##### Math Reasoning.

We evaluate on four math benchmarks of varying difficulty.
MATH-500 ([Hendrycks et al., 2021](#bib.bib20); [Lightman et al.,
2024](#bib.bib35)) contains 500 competition-level problems drawn from
the MATH dataset, spanning algebra, geometry, number theory, and
calculus. AMC 2023 contains problems from the American Mathematics
Competition. AIME 2024 ([Mathematical Association of America,
2024](#bib.bib27)) and AIME 2025 ([Mathematical Association of America,
2025](#bib.bib28)) contain 30 problems each from the American
Invitational Mathematics Examination—a high-difficulty competition where
mode collapse on reasoning trajectories is particularly punitive.

##### Code Generation.

We evaluate on four code synthesis benchmarks. HumanEval ([Chen et al.,
2021](#bib.bib32)) and MBPP ([Austin et al., 2021](#bib.bib34)) are
canonical Python function synthesis benchmarks. HumanEval+ and MBPP+
([Liu et al., 2023](#bib.bib33)) extend the original benchmarks with
substantially more rigorous test cases, exposing solutions that pass the
original tests via shortcuts.

### D.2 Models

##### Creative Writing.

We evaluate two open-weight instruction-tuned models from different
families to test cross-family generalization: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ([Yang
et al., 2024](#bib.bib2)) and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct ([Dubey et al.,
2024](#bib.bib1)). As additional reference points, we report scores from
larger instruction-tuned models (Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct and
Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct) under default sampling at $`T=0.9`$.

##### Math and Code Reasoning.

All reasoning experiments are built on Llama-3.1-8B-Base ([Dubey et al.,
2024](#bib.bib1)). We first conduct a warm-up SFT stage using a mixture
of Ultra-Chat ([Ding et al., 2023](#bib.bib36)) (for general
instruction-following) and reasoning data distilled from
Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (for math and code), yielding our *Base*
checkpoint. All subsequent SFT and PRISM variants are fine-tuned from
this Base checkpoint.

### D.3 Baselines

##### Creative Writing.

We compare PRISM against five baselines spanning vanilla sampling,
training-time, and inference-time interventions:

- •
  Vanilla ($`T=0.9`$): Direct sampling from the instruction-tuned model
  without any modification.
- •
  SFT: Fine-tuning on the same multi-teacher candidate pool used by
  PRISM, but without submodular curation (random sampling of 4
  trajectories per prompt) and without noise injection. This isolates
  the contribution of PRISM’s two components.
- •
  NEFTune ([Jain et al., 2023a](#bib.bib14)) ($`\alpha=5`$): A
  training-time embedding noise method designed as a regularizer for
  instruction tuning. We use the canonical $`\alpha=5`$ setting
  recommended by the authors. Critically, NEFTune is trained on the same
  submodular-curated multi-teacher data as PRISM, so the comparison
  isolates the contribution of (a) noise scope (all tokens vs. special
  tokens only) and (b) inference-time noise injection (NEFTune turns
  noise off at inference, PRISM keeps it on).
- •
  VS-Standard ([Zhang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib45)) ($`K=5`$): An
  inference-time prompting method that elicits $`K=5`$ diverse
  candidates in a single forward pass via verbalized instruction.
- •
  FIRE ([Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib41)) ($`T_{1}=30`$, top-$`k=40`$):
  An inference-time decoding method that applies a sharp first-token
  temperature spike followed by regular sampling, trading early-token
  diversity for downstream coherence.

##### Math and Code Reasoning.

For reasoning, we compare against the Base checkpoint (warm-up SFT only)
and SFT (Base + standard supervised fine-tuning on randomly sampled
solutions, controlling for token count against PRISM’s training data).
We also compare PRISM against the following baselines:

- •
  Diverse Beam Search (DBS)  ([Vijayakumar et al., 2016](#bib.bib9)): An
  inference-time decoding method that augments standard beam search with
  a diversity-promoting objective across beam groups. We apply DBS to
  both Llama-3.1-8B-Base (with warm-up) and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct.
- •
  GEM  ([Li et al., 2024](#bib.bib13)): A training-time SFT algorithm
  that modifies the supervised objective to prevent over-memorization
  and preserve output diversity. We apply GEM to Llama-3.1-8B-Base with
  the same randomly-sampled training data as the SFT baseline and
  default hyperparameters from the original paper.

### D.4 Artifact Licenses and Terms of Use

To ensure ethical usage and compliance, we explicitly document the
licensing and distribution terms for all artifacts (datasets and models)
utilized in this work.

##### Datasets.

For reasoning and coding evaluation, we utilize the MATH and HumanEval
benchmarks under the MIT License, while MBPP is used under CC-BY 4.0.
The extended EvalPlus benchmarks (HumanEval+ and MBPP+) are distributed
under the Apache 2.0 License. The AMC and AIME competition problems are
copyrighted educational resources by the Mathematical Association of
America (MAA) and are evaluated here exclusively for non-commercial,
academic research. For creative writing, BookMIA utilizes copyrighted
book snippets strictly under fair use for research evaluation, and the
WritingPrompts dataset is utilized under its original research-only
distribution terms provided by FAIR. For model training, the Ultra-Chat
dataset is used in accordance with the MIT License.

##### Models.

We employ the Qwen2.5 open-weight models (7B and 72B) under the Apache
2.0 License. The Llama-3.1 models (8B, 70B, and Base variants) are
strictly used in accordance with the Llama 3.1 Community License
Agreement. Furthermore, reasoning trajectories distilled from
Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct to fine-tune the Base model comply with Meta’s
acceptable use policy, which permits using outputs to improve other
Llama models. All artifacts are employed consistently with their
intended research purposes and no proprietary content is redistributed.

### D.5 Hyperparameters

For PRISM’s noise injection, the standard deviation of the Gaussian
noise is set to $`\sigma=0.005`$ for creative writing and
$`\sigma=0.01`$ for reasoning, an order of magnitude smaller than the
typical embedding norm so that the perturbation remains a controllable
signal rather than a disruptive one. We provide a sensitivity analysis
of the injected noise in appendix
[E](#A5 "Appendix E Sensitivity to the Noise Magnitude 𝜎 ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation").
The noise is injected only on the embeddings of special structural
tokens, specifically the begin/end-of-sequence and turn-boundary
tokens—and never on ordinary content tokens. Concretely, for Llama-3
models the perturbed set is $`\{`$\<\|begin_of_text\|\>,
\<\|end_of_text\|\>, \<\|start_header_id\|\>, \<\|end_header_id\|\>,
\<\|eom_id\|\>, \<\|eot_id\|\>$`\}`$, and for Qwen models it is
$`\{`$\<\|endoftext\|\>, \<\|im_start\|\>, \<\|im_end\|\>$`\}`$. At each
forward pass, an independent noise vector is freshly sampled for every
occurrence of these tokens; the noise is applied during both training
and inference. The default sampling temperature is $`0.3`$ for the
reasoning tasks and $`0.9`$ for creative writing.

## Appendix E Sensitivity to the Noise Magnitude $`\sigma`$

A natural concern is whether PRISM is sensitive to the noise standard
deviation $`\sigma`$. We sweep $`\sigma\in\{0.001,0.005,0.01,0.05\}`$
while holding all other settings fixed, and report diversity and quality
on WritingPrompts with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct.

To interpret these values, note that the *effective* perturbation
magnitude is $`\sigma\sqrt{d}`$ rather than $`\sigma`$ itself, since
$`\mathbf{n}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I_{d})`$ has expected norm
$`\sigma\sqrt{d}`$. For Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct($`d=3584`$, mean
token-embedding norm $`\approx 0.79`$), the swept range spans noise
norms from roughly $`8\%`$ to $`380\%`$ of a typical token embedding.

| $`\sigma`$ | Noise norm        | Diversity $`\uparrow`$ | Quality $`\uparrow`$ |
|------------|-------------------|------------------------|----------------------|
| no noise   | $`0\%`$           | $`30.2`$               | $`37.1`$             |
| $`0.001`$  | $`\approx 8\%`$   | $`32.2`$               | $`38.9`$             |
| $`0.005`$  | $`\approx 38\%`$  | $`41.4`$               | $`\mathbf{51.0}`$    |
| $`0.01`$   | $`\approx 76\%`$  | $`43.6`$               | $`45.3`$             |
| $`0.05`$   | $`\approx 380\%`$ | $`\mathbf{45.7}`$      | $`34.0`$             |

Table 6: Sensitivity of PRISM to $`\sigma`$ on WritingPrompts
(Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct). Diversity rises monotonically while quality
follows an inverted-U; $`\sigma=0.005`$ is used in the main experiments.

Table [6](#A5.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Appendix E Sensitivity to the Noise Magnitude 𝜎 ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation")
shows a clean inverted-U in quality alongside monotonically rising
diversity. At small $`\sigma`$ ($`\sigma=0.001`$, $`\approx 8\%`$ of a
typical token embedding), the perturbation is too weak to act as a
discriminative signal: different noise realizations look nearly
identical to the model, and the resulting outputs barely shift away from
the no-noise baseline (diversity $`32.2`$ vs. $`30.2`$). At large
$`\sigma`$ ($`\sigma=0.05`$, $`\approx 380\%`$), the perturbation
overwhelms the underlying token embedding, corrupting the semantic
content of the prompt itself rather than steering generation among valid
completions; quality collapses below the no-noise baseline ($`34.0`$ vs.
$`37.1`$) even as raw diversity continues to rise. The optimum at
$`\sigma=0.005`$ therefore reflects a principled balance—large enough to
function as a learnable navigation signal, small enough to preserve the
prompt’s semantic identity. Crucially, PRISM is not brittle to this
choice: the window $`\sigma\in[0.001,0.01]`$ all yield strict Pareto
improvements over no-noise, and $`\sigma`$ admits a simple selection
criterion—monitor quality and pick the largest $`\sigma`$ before it
starts to drop.

## Appendix F Fintune Backbone Details

##### Framework.

For training, we employ Llama-Factory ([Zheng et al., 2024](#bib.bib19))
as the LLM training platform.
Table [7](#A6.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Framework. ‣ Appendix F Fintune Backbone Details ‣ PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation")
shows our training hyperparameters in supervised fine-tuning.

| Parameter        | Value  |
|------------------|--------|
| Train batch size | 64     |
| Learning rate    | 5.0e-5 |
| Number of epochs | 1.0    |
| LR scheduler     | cosine |
| Warmup ratio     | 0.1    |
| Precision        | bf16   |

Table 7: Hyperparameters for supervised fine-tuning.

##### Data.

For creative writing, we draw 10000 prompts from the
WritingPrompts ([Fan et al., 2018](#bib.bib42)) and BookMIA ([Shi et
al., 2023](#bib.bib43)) training splits, holding out all evaluation
prompts throughout. For each prompt, we collect candidate continuations
from 8 teacher models (GPT-OSS-120B, GPT-OSS-20B, DeepSeek-V4-Flash-Max,
Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct, Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct, Qwen-2.5-72B, Qwen3-32B,
Qwen3.5-27B), discard low-quality drafts with a reward-model
threshold(Quality score below 30), and use SBERT-feature submodular
optimization to select 4 diverse-yet-high-quality completions per
prompt. For math, we sample 10000 problems from A-m-team verified
data ([Tian et al., 2025](#bib.bib37)) with mid-range cross-model
accuracy ($`33\%`$–$`67\%`$) and use n-gram submodular optimization to
select 4 diverse answers per problem. For code, we draw from four
sources: A-m-team distilled solutions, $`\sim`$3100 LeetCode problems
(32 solutions per problem, 8 selected), OpenCoder SFT-Stage-2
educational-instruct ([Huang et al., 2024](#bib.bib21)) solutions from
Qwen-2.5-Coder-32B (pass rate $`<\!90\%`$, 4 selected), and a broader
OpenCoder mix (Evol-Instruct, McEval-Instruct, Package-Instruct) for
general coding ability. Code submodular selection uses both n-gram and
AST features. Baseline datasets randomly sample 4 solutions per problem
to control for token count.

## Appendix H Human Check Results

In this section, we provide detailed information about the protocol for
our human evaluation on the diversity of the training datasets.

##### Human Evaluators.

The human evaluators were selected based on their strong academic
backgrounds and expertise in mathematical and informatics olympiads.
This rigorous background ensured they possessed the necessary skills to
critically analyze the logical and methodical structure of each
solution, thereby guaranteeing the correctness and reliability of our
human evaluation.

##### Human Verification Protocols.

Two code solutions are considered distinct methods only if they meet one
of the following criteria:

1.  1.
    Algorithm. The core algorithms used in the solutions are different.
    For example, one solution might use a recursive approach while
    another uses an iterative one. Similarly, a Breadth-First Search
    (BFS) is distinct from a Depth-First Search (DFS).
2.  2.
    Data Structure. The solutions employ the same algorithm but apply it
    to different data structures. For instance, an algorithm designed
    for a linked list is considered different from one for a graph, as
    are those tailored for different tree structures.
3.  3.
    Complexity. The solutions have different time complexity. A solution
    with $`O(n)`$ complexity is treated as a distinct method from one
    with $`O(\log n)`$ complexity.

Two math solutions are considered distinct methods only if one of the
following criteria is met:

1.  1.
    Distinct Theorems or Lemmas: The final solutions rely on different
    theorems or lemmas. The use of a theorem in a failed attempt or a
    side note does not count.
2.  2.
    Fundamentally Different Approaches: The solutions employ clearly
    different proof techniques or methods, such as mathematical
    induction versus proof by contradiction.

## Appendix I LLM-As-Judge Pipeline

##### Predefined Algorithms Pool.

To create a curated and representative set of algorithms for our
analysis, we first randomly sampled 1,000 model-generated answers. We
then employed Gemini 2.5 Pro as a judge to analyze the algorithmic
approach of each answer. This process involved prompting the large
language model to identify and categorize the algorithms used. Following
this, Gemini was utilized to aggregate the identified algorithms, which
ultimately yielded a pool of 39 distinct and commonly used algorithms
for our study.

## Appendix J Case Study

### J.1 Creative Writing: A Case Study in Narrative Diversity

To qualitatively illustrate how PRISM expands the space of narrative
trajectories explored by the model on open-ended generation, we examine
a prompt from WritingPrompts, drawing ten independent samples from each
of SFT and PRISM (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct).

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The contrast is striking. SFT collapses onto a single narrative
template: every sample reaches for the same sentimental-reunion arc,
with variation confined to surface-level naming and pacing. PRISM, in
contrast, treats the same prompt as an opening to four distinct generic
framings — epistolary mystery, speculative time-loop, detective
thriller, and quiet literary meditation — each grounded in a different
choice of what kind of story the letter implies.

This pattern exemplifies the mechanism behind PRISM’s shift of the
quality–diversity Pareto frontier: rather than clustering ten samples
onto a single sentimental template, PRISM produces a population of
narratives whose union covers structurally distinct regions of the story
space, providing the richer semantic variation captured by our diversity
metric while preserving per-sample quality.

### J.2 Math Reasoning: A Case Study in Solution Diversity

To qualitatively illustrate how PRISM expands the space of solution
strategies explored by the model, we examine an optimization problem
from MATH500, drawing ten independent samples from each of SFT and
PRISM.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The contrast is striking. SFT collapses onto a single procedural
template: every sample reaches for the same substitution-based recipe,
with variation confined to surface-level computational detail. PRISM, in
contrast, treats the same prompt as an opening to four distinct
mathematical framings — direct substitution in $`x`$, inverse
substitution in $`y`$, variable transformation via $`t=x^{2}`$, and a
vertex-based geometric heuristic — each grounded in a different
reformulation of the optimization problem.

This pattern exemplifies the mechanism behind PRISM’s broader test-time
exploration: rather than clustering ten samples onto a single solution
template, PRISM produces a population of candidates whose union covers
structurally distinct regions of the solution manifold, providing the
richer search space that drives its Pass@N gains.

### J.3 Code Generation: A Case Study in Algorithmic Diversity

To qualitatively illustrate how PRISM expands the space of solution
strategies explored by the model, we examine a combinatorial counting
problem from MBPP, drawing the full budget of $`N=256`$ independent
samples from each of SFT and PRISM.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The contrast is striking. SFT collapses onto a single procedural
template: every one of its $`256`$ samples reaches for the same
summation-based recipe, with variation confined to surface-level
computational detail, and this monoculture is brittle — it yields a
correct program only once. PRISM, in contrast, treats the same prompt as
an opening to ten distinct algorithmic framings — bottom-up tabulation,
top-down memoized recursion, closed-form combinatorial counting, and
beyond — each grounded in a different computational principle.

This pattern exemplifies the mechanism behind PRISM’s broader test-time
exploration: rather than clustering its samples onto a single solution
template, PRISM produces a population of candidates whose union covers
structurally distinct regions of the solution manifold. Crucially, this
diversity is not merely cosmetic — by spanning multiple algorithmic
routes, PRISM raises the chance that at least one sample lands on a
correct implementation, lifting the success rate on this query from
$`0.4\%`$ to $`11.6\%`$ and providing the richer search space that
drives its Pass@N gains.
